# Military leaders
## The prescribed subject
Military leaders is a Paper 1 prescribed subject with two case studies: Genghis Khan (c1200–1227) and Richard I of England (1173–1199). It looks at leadership, campaigns, military strategy and the impact of these leaders.

## Case studies
Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes in 1206 and built an empire through cavalry warfare, mobility, discipline, psychological terror and the decimal organization of his army. Richard I, known as the Lionheart, led the Third Crusade (1189–1192), won the Battle of Arsuf, failed to retake Jerusalem and agreed the Treaty of Jaffa with Saladin.

## Working with sources
Paper 1 uses four sources on the prescribed subject. The origin of a source is who made it, when and where; its purpose is why it was made; its content is what it says. Value and limitation are judged from origin, purpose and content (OPCVL). A primary source is a source created at the time; a secondary source is a later interpretation.

## Key terms
Genghis Khan: founder of the Mongol Empire, united the tribes in 1206
Richard I: King of England and a leader of the Third Crusade
Third Crusade: the crusade of 1189–1192 to retake Jerusalem
Treaty of Jaffa: the 1192 truce between Richard I and Saladin
Primary source: a source created at the time

# Conquest and its impact
## The prescribed subject
Conquest and its impact is a Paper 1 prescribed subject with two case studies: the final stages of Muslim rule in Spain (1482–1492) and the conquest of Mexico and Peru (1519–1551). It covers the motives for conquest, key events and the impact on conquered peoples.

## Case studies
Ferdinand and Isabella completed the Reconquista with the fall of Granada in 1492. Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec Empire, capturing Tenochtitlan in 1521, helped by indigenous allies such as the Tlaxcalans and by disease. Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire after capturing Atahualpa in 1532. The encomienda system forced indigenous people to work for Spanish settlers.

## Working with sources
Paper 1 uses four sources on the prescribed subject. The origin of a source is who made it, when and where; its purpose is why it was made; its content is what it says. Value and limitation are judged from origin, purpose and content (OPCVL). A primary source is a source created at the time; a secondary source is a later interpretation.

## Key terms
Reconquista: the Christian reconquest of Muslim Spain, completed in 1492
Hernán Cortés: the conquistador who conquered the Aztec Empire
Francisco Pizarro: the conquistador who conquered the Inca Empire
Encomienda: a Spanish system of forced indigenous labour
Tenochtitlan: the Aztec capital, captured in 1521

# The move to global war
## The prescribed subject
The move to global war is a Paper 1 prescribed subject with two case studies: Japanese expansion in East Asia (1931–1941) and German and Italian expansion (1933–1940). It covers causes, events and international responses.

## Case studies
Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931 after the Mukden Incident and left the League of Nations in 1933; the Second Sino-Japanese War began in 1937; the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 brought the USA into the war. Italy invaded Abyssinia in 1935. Germany remilitarized the Rhineland in 1936, carried out the Anschluss with Austria in 1938 and took the Sudetenland after the Munich Agreement. Appeasement was the policy of giving in to demands to avoid war. The Nazi–Soviet Pact (1939) preceded the invasion of Poland.

## Working with sources
Paper 1 uses four sources on the prescribed subject. The origin of a source is who made it, when and where; its purpose is why it was made; its content is what it says. Value and limitation are judged from origin, purpose and content (OPCVL). A primary source is a source created at the time; a secondary source is a later interpretation.

## Key terms
Appeasement: giving in to demands to avoid war
Mukden Incident: the 1931 pretext for Japan’s invasion of Manchuria
Anschluss: Germany’s union with Austria in 1938
Munich Agreement: the 1938 deal giving Germany the Sudetenland
Nazi–Soviet Pact: the 1939 non-aggression pact between Germany and the USSR
League of Nations: the international organization set up after the First World War

# Rights and protest
## The prescribed subject
Rights and protest is a Paper 1 prescribed subject with two case studies: the civil rights movement in the United States (1954–1965) and apartheid South Africa (1948–1964). It covers the nature of discrimination, protests and their results.

## Case studies
Brown v. Board of Education (1954) ruled school segregation unconstitutional. The Montgomery bus boycott (1955–1956), the sit-ins, the Freedom Rides, the March on Washington (1963) and the Selma marches led to the Civil Rights Act (1964) and the Voting Rights Act (1965). Apartheid was the system of racial segregation in South Africa, enforced through laws such as the Population Registration Act and the pass laws. The ANC's Defiance Campaign, the Freedom Charter (1955) and the Sharpeville Massacre (1960) led to the Rivonia Trial and Nelson Mandela's imprisonment in 1964.

## Working with sources
Paper 1 uses four sources on the prescribed subject. The origin of a source is who made it, when and where; its purpose is why it was made; its content is what it says. Value and limitation are judged from origin, purpose and content (OPCVL). A primary source is a source created at the time; a secondary source is a later interpretation.

## Key terms
Brown v. Board of Education: the 1954 ruling against school segregation
Civil Rights Act: the 1964 US law banning discrimination
Apartheid: South Africa’s system of racial segregation
Sharpeville Massacre: police killing of protesters in 1960
Freedom Charter: the 1955 statement of the anti-apartheid movement
Montgomery bus boycott: the 1955–1956 protest against bus segregation

# Conflict and intervention
## The prescribed subject
Conflict and intervention is a Paper 1 prescribed subject with two case studies: Rwanda (1990–1998) and Kosovo (1989–2002). It covers the causes of the conflicts, the course of events, and international intervention.

## Case studies
In Rwanda, tensions between Hutu and Tutsi, shaped by colonial rule, led to civil war in 1990 and the genocide of 1994, in which about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, were killed in about 100 days. The UN peacekeeping mission (UNAMIR) failed to stop it. In Kosovo, Milošević removed Kosovo's autonomy in 1989; conflict between the Kosovo Liberation Army and Serbian forces led to NATO's bombing campaign in 1999, without UN Security Council approval. Humanitarian intervention is the use of force to protect people from mass atrocities.

## Working with sources
Paper 1 uses four sources on the prescribed subject. The origin of a source is who made it, when and where; its purpose is why it was made; its content is what it says. Value and limitation are judged from origin, purpose and content (OPCVL). A primary source is a source created at the time; a secondary source is a later interpretation.

## Key terms
Genocide: the deliberate killing of a national, ethnic or religious group
UNAMIR: the UN peacekeeping mission in Rwanda
Humanitarian intervention: the use of force to protect people from atrocities
Kosovo Liberation Army: the armed group fighting Serbian rule in Kosovo
Slobodan Milošević: the Serbian leader who removed Kosovo’s autonomy

# Society and economy (750–1400)
## The topic
This topic studies medieval societies and economies, including feudalism, religion, trade, towns and the effects of plague. Feudalism was a social system in which land was granted in return for military service and loyalty. Manorialism organized the rural economy around the lord's manor and serf labour.

## Themes
Key themes include the role of the Church and Islam in society, trade networks such as the Silk Roads and the Hanseatic League, the growth of towns and guilds, and the Black Death (1347–1351), which killed perhaps a third of Europe's population and raised wages for survivors.

## Writing Paper 2 essays

Historiography is the study of how historians have interpreted the past.

## Key terms
Feudalism: land granted in return for military service and loyalty
Manorialism: a rural economy based on the lord’s manor and serf labour
Guild: an association of craftsmen or merchants
Black Death: the plague of 1347–1351

# Causes and effects of medieval wars (750–1500)
## The topic
This topic studies the types, causes, practices and effects of medieval wars. Causes include religion, dynastic claims, territory and economic gain. Wars include the Crusades, the Hundred Years' War (1337–1453) between England and France, and the Mongol invasions.

Practices include castles, siege warfare, mounted knights, the longbow and the use of mercenaries. Effects include changes in political power, the growth of national identity, economic damage and the spread of disease and ideas.

# Origins, development and impact of industrialization (1750–2005)
## The topic
Industrialization is the shift from agricultural and handicraft economies to machine-based manufacturing. It began in Britain in the late 18th century because of coal, capital, colonies, agricultural changes and inventions such as the steam engine.

## Impact
Impacts include urbanization, the factory system, new social classes, poor working conditions, the growth of trade unions, and environmental change. Industrialization spread to Germany, the USA, Japan and later to the USSR and China. Key innovations include railways, electricity and mass production.

# Authoritarian states (20th century)
## The topic
This topic studies the emergence, consolidation and maintenance of power in authoritarian states. An authoritarian state is one where power is concentrated in a leader or party not accountable to the people. A totalitarian state seeks to control every aspect of life.

## Case studies
Common case studies include Hitler's Germany, Stalin's USSR, Mao's China, Mussolini's Italy and Castro's Cuba. Leaders came to power through economic crisis, weakness of previous governments, ideology and the use of force. They consolidated power with propaganda, terror, a cult of personality and control of education and the economy.

# The Cold War: superpower tensions and rivalries (20th century)
## The topic
The Cold War was the period of tension between the USA and the USSR from about 1945 to 1991, fought without direct war between them. Causes include ideological differences between capitalism and communism, the breakdown of wartime cooperation and disputes over Europe.

## Key events
Key events include the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan (1947), the Berlin Blockade (1948–1949), the Korean War, the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962), détente in the 1970s and the end of the Cold War in 1989–1991. Containment was the US policy of stopping the spread of communism. Détente was the easing of tensions.

Historical investigation:
# Historical investigation
## The investigation
The historical investigation is the internal assessment, a written piece of up to 2200 words on a historical question of your choice. It has three sections: identification and evaluation of sources, investigation, and reflection.

## Doing it well
Choose a focused research question. In section 1, evaluate two sources in depth using their origin, purpose and content. In section 2, write a structured, analytical argument using a range of evidence and perspectives. In section 3, reflect on the methods historians use and the challenges you faced, linking to knowledge questions. A research question is the focused question the investigation answers.

## Key terms
Historical investigation: the internal assessment on a question of your choice
Research question: the focused question the investigation answers
Reflection: thinking about historians’ methods and challenges
OPCVL: origin, purpose, content, value and limitation
